title: ArborCare Medical — Podcast: Inference at the Heart of Telehealth
summary: A conversational podcast-style interview focusing on how ArborCare integrated Redwood Inference to scale telehealth NLP features. Covers motivation, architecture choices (hosted vs private), latency/cost tradeoffs, security considerations, and marketing impact. Ends with next steps to share audio and short case study draft.
action_items: Aisha Patel: Send final podcast audio and Redwood one-pager by 2027-09-21
Diego Ramirez: Provide simple diagram of inference flow (hosted + VPC fallback) by 2027-09-20
Ruth Alvarez: Approve 1-page case study draft or suggest edits by 2027-09-24
Lena Zhou: Trim interview audio to ~28 minutes and add intro music by 2027-09-18
next_steps: Redwood to deliver edited audio and one-pager
Customer to review and sign off on marketing release
Schedule a short follow-up to confirm publication date
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-14
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Producer), Dr. Maya (CTO, ArborCare), Evan (Head of ML), Ruth (Head of Product), Samir (Marketing)

[00:00] Aisha: Hi everyone, welcome to our little podcast session today, thanks for carving out time. Real casual — we'll kick off with intros and a bit about how you use Redwood, then dig into the technical bits and finish with the story angle.
[00:18] Dr. Maya: Thanks Aisha, excited. I'm Maya, CTO at ArborCare. We run telehealth triage and notes augmentation, basically trying to make clinician workflows less manual.
[00:30] Evan: Hey all, Evan — head of ML. I am the one who fought the model latency demons.
[00:36] Ruth: Ruth here, product. I mostly end up explaining to ops why we need lower latency.
[00:41] Samir: Samir, marketing — I'm focused on the go-to-market impact, case studies, that sort of thing.
[00:47] Aisha: Excellent. Diego and I are from Redwood — Diego is our systems SE who helped onboard you. Diego, quick one-liner?
[00:54] Diego: Yeah hi, I work on inference performance and deployment patterns, happy to nerd out.
[01:00] Lena: I'll be producing this session and we'll turn it into a short podcast and a one-page case study.
[01:07] Aisha: Cool. To kick off, Maya, can you give a short origin story — what problem prompted you to look for an inference platform?
[01:15] Dr. Maya: Sure. So in 2025 we built a prototype using open models for SOAP note generation and triage routing. That worked fine in batch but when we put it in front of clinicians they — like, they'd press a button and wait, and the wait killed adoption. Also cost started to balloon with our initial hosting.
[01:33] Evan: Right, we were seeing 700–900ms p99 for the small LLM on our infra, and token costs weren't compiled with what product wanted. We needed predictable latency and predictable cost.
[01:45] Aisha: And that's where Redwood comes in — can you remember the moment you decided to run a pilot?
[01:50] Ruth: We had a quarterly target, and marketing was ready to roll a pilot, so engineering needed something we could trust. We chose Redwood because of the dedicated capacity option and the promise of the same API across environments.
[02:02] Samir: Also, Redwood's public latency benchmarks were a big factor for convincing stakeholders.
[02:08] Aisha: Nice. Evan, tell us about the architecture you landed on — hosted first or private from day one?
[02:15] Evan: Hosted first. We started on the hosted API to get up fast — ship, measure latency in real-world usage, and then grad shifted to Dedicated pools for peak hours. On the private side we needed VPC peering for PHI later, but that was phase two.
[02:29] Diego: One detail people ask about — you used a hybrid routing policy, right? Traffic goes to Hosted unless load or PHI flags cause a VPC route?
[02:36] Evan: Exactly. We tag requests in the app; low-risk anonymized summarization goes to hosted, anything with patient identifiers routes to our private deployment.
[02:45] Aisha: How did you handle caching for repeated prompts or common templates?
[02:49] Evan: We implemented prefix-KV caching for standard triage prompts. That shaved about 15% off token usage and improved p50 latency by 60ms on average. Diego helped tune the batch sizes.
[03:02] Diego: Yeah, tuning continuous batching across mixed request sizes was the trick. We looked at the sequence length distribution and set dynamic batch windows.
[03:12] Aisha: Was there any surprise in the first month?
[03:15] Dr. Maya: The surprise was how clinicians changed phrasing once the model got good. That broke some of our prompt policies and we had to iterate on evals.
[03:24] Ruth: From a product lens, we underestimated the need for streaming partial responses in some flows — until we turned it on, the UX felt sluggish.
[03:33] Aisha: On security — HIPAA and audit — what were the blockers?
[03:37] Dr. Maya: We needed audit logs, SSO, and KMS integration. Redwood's private offering had the KMS/HSM integrations we needed, and the audit logs were acceptable after a short review.
[03:49] Evan: There was a bit of back-and-forth around retention. Our legal team wanted 30-day token retention for debug but wanted logs anonymized after 90 days. Redwood helped provide configurable retention policies.
[04:02] Aisha: Competitors popped up in your procurement process?
[04:05] Ruth: We reviewed Anthropic and a few public cloud endpoints. Anthropic had good safety features but the cost/latency profile for our mix was worse. OpenAI was very fast for some models but predictable throughput at scale was more expensive.
[04:20] Samir: From our side, the narrative was about reliability and clinician trust — not raw benchmark numbers.
[04:28] Lena: Nice point. For the podcast angle, what anecdotes should we highlight? Any memorable moment?
[04:33] Dr. Maya: One is when a clinician submitted a heavy note and the system returned a suggested follow-up that was so useful she told the patient about it in the same visit — adoption spiked after that.
[04:44] Evan: Another is during a peak outage elsewhere — Redwood's graceful degradation policies fell back to a lighter model and the app kept running, albeit with slightly different phrasing. That saved a pilot demo with an enterprise customer.
[04:58] Aisha: Love those. Can you give us some numbers — latency, cost delta, or adoption?
[05:04] Evan: Sure. After moving critical paths to a dedicated pool and enabling prefix caching, p95 latency dropped from ~1.3s to ~480ms, and cost per 1k tokens decreased around 28% due to batching and cache reductions. Adoption: active clinician usage went from 12% to 42% in two quarters.
[05:21] Ruth: And the support tickets for slow responses dropped by 73%.
[05:25] Aisha: Great metrics. Diego, any notes on quantization or kernel choices that helped?
[05:30] Diego: We evaluated 4-bit quantized variants for the mid-size model — the throughput improved and the output quality remained acceptable for triage tasks after some calibration. The runtime picking optimized kernels based on sequence length distribution mattered a lot; we tuned the thresholds so long sequence notes used a different execution path.
[05:54] Dr. Maya: I love the detail — too geeky for marketing, but valuable for our engineering blog.
[06:01] Aisha: We'll split the content: short podcast for marketing, deeper engineering blog with Diego and Evan.
[06:08] Samir: On the case study draft — we'd like a headline around "Faster notes, happier clinicians" and a pull quote about the adoption bump.
[06:17] Ruth: Agree, and let's reference the p95 improvement and cost savings — but keep exact numbers high-level in public.
[06:25] Aisha: Noted. Switching gears — what was the onboarding time and friction points?
[06:30] Evan: From contract to first production pilot around six weeks. Friction: initial network setup for VPC peering and KMS took a couple of sprints because our security team required extra checks. Once peered, capacity plans were straightforward.
[06:44] Diego: We did a load test that mimicked peak clinic hours and found a few memory pressure issues in the initial rollout; those were patched quickly.
[06:52] Samir: Any unexpected governance asks?
[06:55] Dr. Maya: They asked for data lineage for certain derived outputs — we added metadata headers to responses and stored provenance in our event log.
[07:06] Aisha: Nice — a good nugget for the engineering blog.
[07:09] Lena: For the podcast edit, any off-limits topics or compliance lines we need to avoid?
[07:14] Ruth: Don't use patient names or case identifiers. Also avoid implying Redwood or us provide medical advice — stick to 'workflow augmentation' language.
[07:24] Lena: Got it. We'll keep it generic and compliant.
[07:28] [laughter]
[07:30] Aisha: A fun question: what's the weirdest prompt clinicians used?
[07:33] Evan: One clinician asked the model to "translate into lay and emoji" for a pediatric patient note — and the emoji suggestion was... unexpected.
[07:43] Dr. Maya: We had to block a couple of template prompts that became memetic, they broke the normalization pipeline.
[07:51] Aisha: Haha. Back to production concerns — how do you run experiments and rollouts without disrupting clinicians?
[07:58] Evan: Canary deploys per account group and automatic fallback to a safe model variant. We run A/B on a random subset and have automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions. Redwood's rollout hooks made that simple.
[08:12] Diego: Also use closed eval sets tied to specific prompt categories and label noise rejection in preflight.
[08:20] Ruth: The team keeps a "golden prompt" suite — we run it every build.
[08:25] Aisha: On the business side, how did procurement and contract negotiation go? Any tips?
[08:31] Ruth: We had standard enterprise concerns: SLAs, liability caps, data use terms. Redwood was flexible with dedicated capacity commitments and offered a pilot clause which helped.
[08:44] Samir: For marketing we needed permission to use metrics and logos — legal signed the release after a short review.
[08:50] Aisha: Good. Any regrets or things you'd do differently?
[08:54] Dr. Maya: Start the privacy review earlier. That would have removed one stall.
[08:59] Evan: More stress testing on mixed short and long sequences before the pilot; that would've saved a week.
[09:06] Aisha: Great advice. What about team org changes post-integration?
[09:10] Ruth: We created a small "Inference Ops" team inside ML to manage models and prompts; formerly those tasks were split across infra and ML. Consolidation helped velocity.
[09:20] Samir: Marketing also embedded an engineer for two sprints to get story fidelity. That helped quickly craft the case study.
[09:27] Aisha: Love the cross-functional story. We're about 9 minutes in, do we want to take a quick break or keep rolling?
[09:35] Dr. Maya: Keep going, we're good.
[09:37] Aisha: OK. For the engineering blog, Diego, can you briefly outline the most surprising optimization?
[09:43] Diego: The biggest win was prefix caching combined with dynamic batching and model variant routing. It wasn't any single optimization — it was the combination. We saw diminishing returns if you only did one.
[09:56] Evan: Also, aligning kernel selection to input distribution was low-effort high-impact. When we shifted the long notes to a different kernel path p95 improved for the entire flow.
[10:08] Aisha: Any tooling you built on top of Redwood?
[10:12] Evan: We built a thin adapter that tags requests, handles redaction for hosted paths, and routes by sensitivity. Also a dashboard that maps cost per feature.
[10:22] Ruth: That dashboard was crucial for leadership; it connected product KPIs to spend.
[10:27] Aisha: On the topic of quality monitoring and evals — how often do you run them?
[10:32] Evan: Nightly automated evals on a curated set, and a weekly human-in-the-loop review for edge cases. If the regression alert fires we block deploys.
[10:42] Aisha: That's solid. Audience question from our pre-submitted list — how did the clinician training change after launching?
[10:48] Dr. Maya: We added 20 minutes of micro-training in the EHR onboarding and a one-pager of do's and don'ts. That reduced misuse and improved prompt formulations.
[10:59] Samir: And we created a quick video that marketing used to show real examples (anonymized).
[11:06] Aisha: Okay, let's capture three short soundbites for the podcast — Maya, a sentence about impact; Evan, a sentence about technical win; Samir, a sentence about what this means for patients.
[11:15] Dr. Maya: "We shipped inference that actually made clinicians' days shorter — and that means more time with patients."
[11:25] Evan: "By combining caching, dynamic batching, and dedicated capacity we cut our p95 latency in half and reduced cost per request."
[11:33] Samir: "For patients it translates to faster follow-ups and clearer communication — small changes, big trust wins."
[11:43] Lena: Perfect, we'll use those as pull quotes.
[11:46] [sound of coffee cup clink]
[11:48] Aisha: Quick logistical — Lina sorry, Lena — can I get a preferred headline? Samir mentioned one earlier but any tweaks?
[11:56] Samir: "Faster Notes, Better Care: How ArborCare Scaled Inference for Telehealth" — but maybe we shorten to "Faster Notes, Better Care" for social.
[12:06] Ruth: Works for me. Keep the subhead about the p95 improvement.
[12:11] Aisha: Great. Any customer-facing quotes that need approval? Ruth?
[12:15] Ruth: I'll review with legal and return a one-line approval in writing.
[12:20] Aisha: Action noted. Switching back to subtle technical stuff — storage of KV cache and backup strategy?
[12:26] Evan: We store ephemeral KV in the serving layer; persisted checkpoints in encrypted blob storage. Cache warmup scripts prefetch common prefixes at peak start times.
[12:37] Diego: We also use a small local hot-cache on the host to avoid remote RTTs for very common prefixes.
[12:44] Dr. Maya: That hot-cache prevented a lot of small latency spikes.
[12:49] Aisha: Cool. Two more big-picture questions: how did this affect roadmap priorities and where do you go next?
[12:56] Ruth: We accelerated features around guided documentation and clinician suggestions. Next: multimodal notes with image inputs for wound care, but that raises new privacy and compute questions.
[13:09] Evan: We're also working on on-prem or air-gapped options for hospitals that require it; Redwood's private deployment path makes that feasible.
[13:18] Aisha: And any metrics you plan to share publicly beyond the case study?
[13:22] Samir: We'll share adoption % and high-level latency improvement, but financials will stay internal.
[13:29] Aisha: Understood. A few candid questions from our producer — any parting challenges or war stories?
[13:36] Evan: War story: we once had a template that exploded token counts because of an accidental infinite recursion in a prompt loop — we added guardrails.
[13:45] Dr. Maya: And we learned to have QA prompts that intentionally try to break the model.
[13:50] Lena: Love these for the behind-the-scenes blog.
[13:53] Aisha: We're approaching the end — any final advice for other healthtech startups evaluating Redwood or similar platforms?
[14:00] Ruth: Do a hybrid pilot: start hosted for speed, iterate, then move sensitive workloads to private.
[14:07] Evan: Focus on input distribution analysis early; it drives kernel and batching decisions.
[14:12] Dr. Maya: Bring security and legal to the table early.
[14:17] Aisha: Solid. OK, closing items: Aisha recap and next steps.
[14:21] Aisha: We'll produce the ~28-minute podcast edit and a one-page Redwood/ArborCare one-pager. Diego will share a technical diagram. Ruth will sign off copy. Lena will deliver audio by the dates in the action items. Anything to add?
[14:36] Ruth: No, that covers it.
[14:38] Samir: One ask — include a short b-roll of clinicians anonymized for marketing if possible.
[14:43] Aisha: Noted. We'll coordinate.
[14:45] Lena: I'll reach out separately for assets.
[14:48] Aisha: Awesome. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in Slack.
[14:52] Dr. Maya: Thanks, talk soon.
[14:54] Evan: Thanks!
[14:55] Ruth: Bye.
[14:57] Samir: Bye.

[END]
